definition: Combative means eager or ready to fight, argue, or resist.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word combative. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know combative should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The panelist turned combative in the first five minutes, interrupting every answer with a challenge.
Assertive is weaker than combative: an assertive person states positions firmly but fairly, while a combative one turns every exchange into a fight.
Warlike is stronger than combative — warlike suggests readiness for open, organized battle, while combative describes a person's argumentative, fight-seeking manner.

Belligerent means openly hostile and aggressive — in formal use it literally names a nation waging war. Combative is smaller and more personal: an argument-picking, fight-seeking manner in ordinary exchanges. A belligerent power mobilizes armies; a combative neighbor turns a fence question into a feud.

Quarrelsome names a petty habit: a quarrelsome person bickers over small things wherever they go. Combative is stronger and more deliberate — eager for the confrontation itself, ready to fight or resist head-on rather than merely squabble. Quarrelsome grumbles over trifles; combative goes looking for the battle.

The budget hearing was supposed to be routine.
Instead, the new council member contested the very first line item, demanded the treasurer defend a decade-old decision, and challenged the chair's right to limit her speaking time — twice.
When a colleague offered a compromise, she called it surrender.
Observers agreed the council had gained its most combative member in memory.
Contesting every item, challenging the chair, and treating compromise as surrender show someone actively spoiling for a fight — the eagerness to battle that combative names.

Reporters covering the Harbor City hockey club learned to brace for coach Renata Voss's press conferences.
She was combative from the opening question — disputing premises, demanding sources, and turning queries about line changes into arguments about the reporters' preparation.
Colleagues insisted the manner was strategy rather than temper: every minute the press spent sparring with her was a minute her players escaped scrutiny.
Off camera, the beat writers noted, she answered the same questions patiently and at length.
The performance ended when the team started winning; with nothing left to deflect, her podium answers turned brief and mild.
